title: Home regulator outside IOSCO
fact1_value: Halden Value Fund, a regulated fund
fact2_value: Not an IOSCO MMoU (Appendix A) signatory, and no bilateral MoU with SEBI
fact3_value: Its home country, not an IFSC
question: Can the DDP register it?
option_A: Yes, as Category II
option_B: No. It fails the home-regulator test in Reg 4(d)
option_C: Yes, if its manager is from a FATF member country
option_D: Yes, as Category I, because it is regulated
explanation: Reg 4(d) requires the applicant to be resident in a country whose securities regulator has signed the IOSCO MMoU (Appendix A) or has a bilateral MoU with SEBI. The two exceptions are a government investor from a country approved by the Government of India, and an applicant set up in an IFSC.
why_not_A: Choosing a category doesn't cure eligibility. Reg 4 applies to every category, so Category II is still blocked.
why_not_C: The FATF-manager test only helps an applicant get into Category I under Reg 5. It doesn't override Reg 4(d).
why_not_D: Being regulated affects the category, but the applicant has to pass Reg 4(d) first.
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 4(d)
quote_1: (d) the applicant is a resident of the country whose securities market regulator is a signatory to the International Organization of Securities Commission's Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding (Appendix A Signatories) or a signatory to the bilateral Memorandum of Understanding with the Board: Provided that an applicant being Government or Government related investor shall be considered as eligible for registration, if such applicant is a resident in the country as may be approved by the Government of India;
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 4(d) and proviso; Op. Guidelines Part A 2(i)

title: Bank whose central bank isn't in the BIS
fact1_value: Commercial bank, licensed by its home banking regulator
fact2_value: Not a member of the Bank for International Settlements
fact4_value: Category I, as a regulated bank
question: Where does this applicant land?
option_A: Category I, as a bank regulated by its home banking regulator
option_B: Category II, which the guidelines allow for such banks
option_C: Not eligible in any category, because of the BIS test
option_D: Category I, once RBI approves the application
explanation: A bank applicant is expected to come from a country whose central bank is a BIS member (Reg 4(e)). The guidelines let a bank regulated at home whose central bank isn't a BIS member seek registration under Category II instead.
why_not_A: Category I for a bank assumes its central bank is a BIS member, which isn't the case here.
why_not_C: Too strict. The guidelines expressly let this bank apply under Category II.
why_not_D: No RBI approval converts this into Category I. RBI is consulted only for banks with an Indian presence.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 3(i)
quote_1: In case a bank FPI applicant is regulated by the banking sector regulator in its home jurisdiction, but the central bank of that country is not a member of BIS, the FPI can seek registration under Category II.
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 4(e); Op. Guidelines Part A 3(i)

title: Foreign bank with an Indian branch
fact1_value: Proprietary investment arm of a European bank
fact2_value: The bank has a branch in Mumbai
question: What extra step applies before you register it?
option_A: None. Process it like any other Category I bank
option_B: Send it to SEBI first, which gets RBI's comments
option_C: Ask the applicant to get RBI's approval directly
option_D: Register it now, then tell RBI within 7 working days of approval
explanation: When the applicant or its group entity is a bank with a branch or representative office in India, or is a central bank, the DDP sends the form to SEBI. SEBI asks RBI for comments and passes them to the DDP to consider. This isn't repeated at continuance.
why_not_A: The Indian branch triggers a reference to SEBI and RBI. Skipping it is a process breach.
why_not_C: The DDP routes the form through SEBI. The applicant doesn't go to RBI itself.
why_not_D: RBI's comments come before registration, not after it.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 3(i)
quote_1: In case an applicant/ its group entity is (i) bank or its subsidiary and has a bank branch/representative office in India or (ii) a central bank or its subsidiary, the respective DDP shall forward the application form to SEBI. SEBI would in turn request RBI to provide its comments. Based on the comments received from RBI, SEBI would notify the comments of RBI to DDP to consider while processing such applications.

title: Unregulated Luxembourg partnership
fact2_value: Unregulated limited partnership
fact3_value: Luxembourg AIFM, appropriately regulated, registered with SEBI as a Category I FPI
fact4_value: Manager accepts responsibility for the fund's acts and omissions
question: Which category?
option_A: Category I
option_B: Category II, because the fund itself is unregulated
option_C: Not eligible
option_D: Category II until the fund is regulated
explanation: Under Reg 5(a)(iv)(II), an unregulated fund from a FATF member country is Category I when its manager is appropriately regulated, is registered as a Category I FPI, and takes responsibility for the fund's acts and omissions. Luxembourg is a FATF member.
why_not_B: Reg 5(a)(iv)(II) lets an unregulated fund from a FATF country take Category I through a regulated Category I manager.
why_not_C: Unregulated funds can register. Reg 5(b)(viii) even lists them under Category II.
why_not_D: Category I is available now, without the fund being regulated.
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 5(a)(iv)
quote_1: (iv) Entities from the Financial Action Task Force member countries , or from any country specified by the Central Government by an order or by way of an agreement or treaty with other sovereign Governments, which are – I. appropriately regulated funds; II. unregulated funds whose investment manager is appropriately regulated and registered as a Category I foreign portfolio investor: Provided that the investment manager undertakes the responsibility of all the acts of commission or omission of such unregulated fund;

title: Cayman fund, New York manager
fact1_value: Halcyon Opportunities Fund Ltd, Cayman Islands
fact2_value: Unregulated
fact3_value: New York adviser, registered with SEBI as a Category I FPI
fact4_value: Manager accepts responsibility for the fund
question: Which category?
option_A: Category II, because Cayman isn't a FATF member
option_B: Category I, under Reg 5(a)(v)(A)
option_C: Not eligible
option_D: Category I only if Cayman regulates the fund
explanation: Reg 5(a)(v)(A) looks at the manager, not where the fund sits. An entity whose manager is from a FATF member country and is registered as a Category I FPI qualifies for Category I, provided the manager takes responsibility. Without that registration and undertaking, the fund would fall to Category II.
why_not_A: That would be right under Reg 5(a)(iv), which looks at the fund's country. Reg 5(a)(v)(A) looks at the manager's.
why_not_C: Nothing here fails the Reg 4 eligibility tests, and unregulated funds can register.
why_not_D: The fund doesn't need to be regulated. The manager route gives Category I.
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 5(a)(v)
quote_1: (v) An entity (A) whose investment manager is from the Financial Action Task Force member country and such an investment manager is registered as a Category I foreign portfolio investor; or (B) which is at least seventy-five per cent owned, directly or indirectly by another entity, eligible under sub-clause (ii), (iii) and (iv) of clause (a) of this regulation and such an eligible entity is from a Financial Action Task Force member country: Provided that such an investment manager or eligible entity undertakes the responsibility of all the acts of commission or omission of the applicants seeking registration under this sub-clause.

title: NRI general partner runs the fund
fact2_value: 20% of the corpus
fact4_value: An NRI is the general partner. The manager isn't registered with SEBI.
question: Is the applicant eligible?
option_A: Yes. Both percentages are inside the limits
option_B: No. NRIs can't be in control of the applicant
option_C: Yes, but only if it registers as a Category II FPI instead
option_D: No. Total NRI money has to stay under 25%
explanation: Three tests apply: each NRI, OCI or RI below 25%, all of them together below 50%, and none of them in control. The control test has carve-outs: an offshore fund with a SEBI NOC under the Mutual Fund Regulations, or a manager controlled by NRIs that is regulated at home and registered with SEBI as a non-investing FPI, or set up and registered in India. None applies here.
why_not_A: The percentages pass, but the control test fails. All three tests have to be met.
why_not_C: The control test is an eligibility condition, so changing the category doesn't fix it.
why_not_D: 25% is the cap for a single NRI, OCI or RI. The cap on all of them together is below 50%.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 2(ii)
quote_1: Where NRIs or OCI or RIs are constituents of the applicant – a. the contribution of a single NRI or OCI or RI shall be below twenty-five percent of the total contribution in the corpus of the applicant; b. the aggregate contribution of NRIs, OCIs and RIs shall be below fifty percent of the total contribution in the corpus of the applicant. Explanation: The contribution of RI is permitted, if made through the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) approved by Reserve Bank of India in global funds whose Indian exposure is less than 50%. c. the NRIs, OCIs and RIs shall not be in control of the applicant.
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 4(c); Op. Guidelines Part A 2(ii)(a)–(d)

title: Redemptions push NRI share over 50%
fact2_value: Other investors redeem; NRI/OCI share rises to 53%
question: What timeline applies?
option_A: Sell all Indian holdings within 5 trading days of the breach
option_B: 90 days to fix it, then a purchase block and a 180-day exit
option_C: No action needed, because a passive breach doesn't count
option_D: Stop all trading today and report the breach to SEBI
explanation: A temporary breach of the NRI/OCI/RI limits gives the FPI 90 days to comply again. If it is still in breach after 90 days, it can't make fresh purchases and must sell its positions within the following 180 days.
why_not_A: 5 trading days is the timeline for breaching an investment limit, not for breaching the investor-mix limits.
why_not_C: A temporary breach still counts. The 90-day period exists to fix exactly this.
why_not_D: Nothing is blocked on day one. The FPI gets 90 days to comply first.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 2(ii)(f)
quote_1: In case of temporary breach of above investment limits after December 31. 2020, the foreign portfolio investor shall comply with the eligibility conditions within ninety days of its breach. In case the foreign portfolio investor remains non-compliant with the said requirement even after ninety days, then no fresh purchases shall be permitted and such foreign portfolio investor shall liquidate its existing position in Indian securities market within a period of the next one hundred and eighty days.

title: Two sister FPIs cross 10% together
fact2_value: Holds 3.5% of Company X
question: What's the position?
option_A: Fine. Each FPI is below 10% on its own, so no breach
option_B: Breach. Sell the excess in 5 trading days or it all becomes FDI
option_C: Fine, as long as the aggregate FPI limit still has room
option_D: Breach, and the exchange reverses B's new purchase to cure it
explanation: Common ownership above 50%, or common control, puts FPIs in one investor group, and their holdings count together against the below-10% limit on a fully diluted basis. If the excess isn't sold within 5 trading days of settlement, the group's entire investment in the company is treated as FDI, and it can't make further portfolio investment in that company.
why_not_A: Common ownership above 50% makes them one investor group, so the limit applies to the combined 10.3%.
why_not_C: The aggregate FPI limit is a separate cap at company level. The 10% group limit still applies.
why_not_D: Exchange trades aren't reversed. The fix is to sell down within 5 trading days, or the holding turns into FDI.
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 20(7)
quote_1: (7) The purchase of equity shares of each company by a single foreign portfolio investor including its investor group shall be below ten per cent of the total paid-up equity capital on a fully diluted basis of the company: Provided that where the total investment under these regulations by a foreign portfolio investor including its investor group exceeds the threshold of below ten per cent of the total paid up equity capital in a listed or to be listed company on a fully diluted basis, the foreign portfolio investor shall divest the excess holding within five trading days from the date of settlement of the trades resulting in the breach: Provided further that in case the foreign portfolio investor fails to divest the excess holding, the entire investment in the company by such foreign portfolio investor including its investor group shall be considered as investment under the Foreign Direct Investment, as per the procedure specified by the Board and the foreign portfolio investor and its investor group shall not make further portfolio investment in that company under these regulations,

title: Two UCITS under one management company
fact1_value: Luxembourg UCITS, holds 6% of Company Y
fact2_value: Irish UCITS, holds 5% of Company Y
fact3_value: Same management company (common control); no common ownership above 50%
question: Are they combined for the 10% limit?
option_A: Yes. Common control makes them one investor group
option_B: No. That rule doesn't apply to regulated public retail funds
option_C: Yes, unless SEBI grants these two funds a specific exemption order
option_D: No, because they are domiciled in different countries
explanation: Reg 22(4) switches off the common-control rule where the FPIs are appropriately regulated public retail funds, or retail funds with regulated managers. The relief covers common control only. If they also shared more than 50% ownership, they would still be combined.
why_not_A: Normally yes, but Reg 22(4) switches off the common-control rule for appropriately regulated public retail funds.
why_not_C: The exemption is written into Reg 22(4) itself. No SEBI order is needed.
why_not_D: Country doesn't decide investor groups. Ownership and control do.
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 22(4)
quote_1: (4) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-regulation (3), the clubbing of investment limit of foreign portfolio investors having common control shall not be applicable where – (a) foreign portfolio investors are appropriately regulated public retail funds; or (b) the foreign portfolio investors are public retail funds where the majority is owned by appropriately regulated public retail fund on look through basis; or (c) foreign portfolio investors are public retail funds and investment managers of such foreign portfolio investors are appropriately regulated. Explanation - Public retail funds means (i) mutual funds or unit trusts which are open for subscription to retail investors and which do not have specific investor type requirements like accredited investors; (ii) insurance companies where segregated portfolio with one to one correlation with a single investor is not maintained; and (iii)pension funds.

title: Ownership change reported eight months late
fact1_value: Category I fund managed by an asset manager
fact2_value: New parent bought 70% of the asset manager on 10 January 2026
question: What does the DDP do?
option_A: Update the records. Late reporting has no consequence
option_B: Re-assess eligibility and report the delay to SEBI
option_C: Cancel the registration for the late intimation
option_D: Block the account permanently for the breach
explanation: Any direct or indirect change in structure, ownership or control must be reported within 7 working days. The DDP has to re-assess eligibility. Where the FPI was more than six months late, the DDP must report the case to SEBI with the reason.
why_not_A: A delay over six months has to go to SEBI, and the change itself needs an eligibility check.
why_not_C: DDPs don't cancel registrations. That is SEBI's decision under the Intermediaries Regulations.
why_not_D: There's no automatic permanent block. The DDP re-assesses eligibility and escalates the delay.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 15
quote_1: In terms of Regulation 22(1)(c), if there is any change in the material information previously furnished by the FPI to the DDP and/or SEBI, which has a bearing on the certificate granted by the DDP on behalf of the Board or relating to any direct or indirect change in its structure or ownership or control, change in regulatory status, merger, demerger or restructuring, change in category/ sub-category / structure/ jurisdiction/ name of FPI/ beneficial ownership etc, of the FPI, it shall forthwith inform the DDP and/or the Board in writing. The DDP shall examine all such material changes and re-assess the eligibility of the FPI including requiring FPIs to seek fresh registration. However, DDP shall not process any request for change in jurisdiction of the FPI and in such cases, FPI may apply for new FPI registration. Where there is a delay of more than six months in intimation of material change by the FPI to the DDP, the DDP shall, forthwith, inform all such cases to SEBI for appropriate action, if any, along with reason for delay.
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 22(1)(c), Reg 31(2)(e); Op. Guidelines Part A 15

title: Fund moves from Dublin to Luxembourg
fact2_value: Redomiciled to Luxembourg
fact3_value: Change the country on the existing registration
question: Can the DDP make the change?
option_A: Yes. Update the registration and its country code
option_B: No. It needs a new FPI registration
option_C: Yes, but only with SEBI's prior written approval
option_D: Yes, because both countries are FATF members
explanation: The DDP re-assesses most material changes, but it can't process a change in the FPI's jurisdiction. The FPI has to apply for a new registration.
why_not_A: The guidelines specifically bar DDPs from processing a change of jurisdiction.
why_not_C: There's no SEBI approval route for this. A fresh registration is the only option.
why_not_D: FATF membership is irrelevant here. A change of jurisdiction can't be processed on an existing registration at all.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 15(ii)
quote_1: The DDP shall examine all such material changes and re-assess the eligibility of the FPI including requiring FPIs to seek fresh registration. However, DDP shall not process any request for change in jurisdiction of the FPI and in such cases, FPI may apply for new FPI registration.

title: Renewal fee paid seven weeks late
fact2_value: 31 August 2026
fact4_value: Take the fee now and continue the registration
question: What do you tell the client?
option_A: Fine. Accept the fee with a written reason for the delay
option_B: Not possible. Surrender, then file a fresh application
option_C: Allowed, since it's still within 90 days of expiry
option_D: Allowed, but only with SEBI's specific permission
explanation: A registration stops being valid after the date fees were paid up to, and continuance can't be applied for after expiry. The entity must surrender and apply fresh. Fees and updates should reach the DDP at least 15 days before validity ends.
why_not_A: A reason for delay covers renewal papers that arrive late but before expiry. After expiry, continuance isn't possible.
why_not_C: There's no 90-day grace period after expiry.
why_not_D: The guidelines give no SEBI permission route. It has to surrender and reapply.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 5
quote_1: Where the FPI has not paid fees for continuance of its registration, its FPI registration shall cease to be valid after the date, up to which, the last registration fees were duly paid by the FPI. An FPI cannot apply for continuance after expiry of its registration. However, if such entity intends to have FPI registration, it will have to make a fresh application for registration after surrender of its earlier FPI registration.
citation: Op. Guidelines Part A 5(iii)–(vi); FPI Regs 2019, Reg 9(3)

title: Broker investing for its clients
fact2_value: Category II, to invest client money
fact3_value: Two individuals, one family office, one trading company
question: Can all four clients invest through this registration?
option_A: Yes. All four would be eligible as FPIs on their own
option_B: No. The trading company can't be a client
option_C: Yes, if the broker also holds a Category I registration
option_D: No. Brokers can't invest on behalf of clients at all
explanation: Regulated entities can invest for clients as Category II FPIs, but those clients must be individuals or family offices, must themselves be eligible as FPIs, and can't act for third parties. Client details go to the DDP every quarter.
why_not_A: Being FPI-eligible is necessary but not enough. The client also has to be an individual or a family office.
why_not_C: A Category I registration covers the broker's own money. It doesn't widen who the client registration can serve.
why_not_D: Regulated entities, brokers included, can invest for clients through a Category II registration.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 3(iv)
quote_1: Where such entities are undertaking investments on behalf of their clients, Category II FPI registration shall be granted subject to following conditions: Clients of FPI can only be individuals and family offices.
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 5(b)(vii); Op. Guidelines Part A 3(iv)

title: Major investor added to UN sanctions list
fact2_value: An investor holding 30% of the corpus is added to the UN Security Council Sanctions List
fact3_value: A sell order on Indian holdings
question: What do you do?
option_A: Block new buys but let the pending sell go through
option_B: Block all buying and selling, and notify SEBI
option_C: Allow trading normally until SEBI writes in
option_D: Freeze only that investor's share of the fund
explanation: If the FPI or a material underlying investor comes under UNSC sanctions, the custodian must stop all further buying and selling in the account and notify SEBI immediately.
why_not_A: Allowing sales is the rule when a home country loses compliant status. Sanctions block selling too.
why_not_C: The custodian acts first and then notifies SEBI. It doesn't wait to hear back.
why_not_D: The block covers the whole FPI account, not one investor's share.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 16(i)
quote_1: Further, in case the FPI itself or its underlying investors contributing twenty-five percent or more in the corpus of the FPI or identified on the basis of control, come under the Sanctions List notified by the United Nations Security Council, custodian shall not allow any further buy/sell in the account of such FPI and shall forthwith notify such instances to SEBI.
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 4(f); Op. Guidelines Part A 16(i)

title: Home country put on the FATF high-risk list
fact2_value: Home country listed in FATF's public statement as high-risk
question: What changes for this FPI?
option_A: It must sell everything within 180 days
option_B: No fresh purchases; it may hold or sell
option_C: The registration is cancelled by the DDP
option_D: Nothing changes until the next renewal
explanation: When a jurisdiction stops being compliant (it leaves IOSCO, a SEBI MoU or the BIS, or FATF names it high-risk), the custodian blocks fresh purchases. The FPI may keep or sell what it holds, and the DDP reports the affected FPIs to SEBI.
why_not_A: There's no forced sale. The FPI can keep or sell its holdings.
why_not_C: The registration isn't cancelled. Fresh purchases are blocked until the jurisdiction is compliant again.
why_not_D: The custodian acts as soon as the status changes, not at renewal.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 16(i)
quote_1: If a jurisdiction, which was a compliant jurisdiction at the time of grant of registration to FPI, becomes non-compliant jurisdiction i.e. ceases to be member of IOSCO/ Bilateral Memorandum of Understanding with SEBI/ BIS or the concerned jurisdiction of FPI is listed in FATF public statement as "high risk" and "noncooperative" jurisdiction or the concerned jurisdiction of FPI then concerned Custodian shall not allow such FPIs to make fresh purchases till the time the jurisdiction/FPI is compliant with the Regulations. However, the FPI shall be allowed to sell the securities or continue to hold the securities already purchased by it. The concerned DDP shall inform to SEBI details of such FPIs upon such change.

title: Rejected for missing papers
fact2_value: DDP A, for incomplete documents and unpaid fee
question: What's the right route?
option_A: Ask SEBI to reconsider within 30 days
option_B: Fix the gaps and reapply, with any DDP
option_C: Wait six months before reapplying anywhere
option_D: Reapply only through DDP A, which rejected it
explanation: An applicant can ask SEBI to reconsider within 30 days, but not when the rejection was technical: missing information or documents, or unpaid fees. Another DDP can take the application once it has checked why it was rejected and confirmed the gaps are fixed.
why_not_A: The 30-day reconsideration route exists, but Reg 8(3) excludes technical rejections like missing documents or fees.
why_not_C: There's no waiting period. It can reapply as soon as the gaps are fixed.
why_not_D: Any DDP can take it, after checking the rejection reason in the depositories' shared database.
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 8(3)
quote_1: (3) The applicant, who is aggrieved by the decision of the designated depository participant under sub-regulation (1) may, within a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of communication under sub-regulation (2), apply to the Board for reconsideration of the decision of the designated depository participant: Provided that such application for reconsideration shall not be considered by the Board where the rejection was on account of technical reasons such as non-submission of complete information, documents, including non-payment of specified fees.
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 8(3); Op. Guidelines Part A 7

title: 30% of a Category III AIF
fact2_value: Subscribe to 30% of a SEBI-registered Category III AIF
question: Can it take the full 30%?
option_A: Yes. Category III AIF units are permitted for FPIs
option_B: No. An FPI can't hold more than 25% in a Category III AIF
option_C: Only with RBI's prior approval for the stake above 25%
option_D: Only Category II FPIs can invest in AIFs
explanation: FPIs can invest in units of Category III AIFs, REITs and InvITs, but a single FPI can't hold more than 25% of a Category III AIF.
why_not_A: They are permitted, but capped at 25% of any one AIF.
why_not_C: No RBI approval lifts the 25% cap.
why_not_D: Both categories can invest in Category III AIF units.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part C 14(ii)
quote_1: A FPI shall not hold more than twenty five percent stake in a category III AIF.
citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 20(1)(e); Op. Guidelines Part C 14

title: Category II fund wants to issue P-notes
fact2_value: Issue offshore derivative instruments on Indian equity
fact3_value: Mix of institutions and wealthy individuals
question: Can it issue these ODIs?
option_A: Yes, as long as it reports them to SEBI monthly
option_B: No. Only Category I FPIs can issue ODIs
option_C: Yes, through a separate ODI-suffixed registration
option_D: Yes, but only to institutional subscribers
explanation: Only Category I FPIs can issue ODIs, only to persons eligible for Category I registration, and only after KYC on the subscribers.
why_not_A: Monthly reporting is a duty of eligible issuers. It doesn't make a Category II FPI eligible.
why_not_C: A separate registration with an "ODI" suffix keeps a Category I issuer's derivatives apart. It doesn't let a Category II FPI issue.
why_not_D: The issuer must be Category I, whoever the subscribers are.
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 21(1)
quote_1: (a) such offshore derivative instruments are issued only by persons registered as Category I foreign portfolio investor; (b) such offshore derivative instruments are issued only to persons eligible for registration as Category I foreign portfolio investors;

title: Surrender with stranded delisted shares
fact2_value: Delisted shares it can't sell on exchange
question: What has to happen first?
option_A: Nothing. Residual shares don't block a surrender
option_B: Get holdings to nil, by off-market sale or write-off
option_C: Transfer the stranded shares to the custodian
option_D: Wait for SEBI to cancel the registration on its own initiative
explanation: The DDP asks SEBI for a no-objection certificate only after confirming nil securities, nil bank balance and nil open derivatives. Delisted shares can be sold off-market under FEMA pricing. If that fails, an FPI that intends to surrender can write them off, reported as a sale with nil proceeds.
why_not_A: The DDP seeks SEBI's no-objection certificate only after confirming nil holdings.
why_not_C: The custodian doesn't take the shares. A write-off removes them from its books and freezes the demat account.
why_not_D: Surrender is a request through the DDP with SEBI's no-objection certificate. Nothing happens automatically.
quote_1_source: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 11(i)
quote_1: DDP shall seek a “No Objection Certificate” (NOC) from the Board to process such surrender after ensuring that the holdings of the concerned applicant in security account and bank account is nil and there are nil outstanding derivative positions.
citation: Op. Guidelines Part A 11; Part C 3(iii) and 17

title: FPI wants shares in an unlisted company
fact2_value: Unlisted Indian fintech
fact4_value: Book it through the FPI account
question: Can this go through the FPI route?
option_A: Yes, because it's well under the 10% limit
option_B: No. Buying unlisted equity is FDI
option_C: Yes, but only with SEBI's prior approval
option_D: Yes, if it's booked as an off-market transfer
explanation: The FPI route covers shares of companies that are listed, or about to be listed, on an Indian exchange. Buying shares in an unlisted company is foreign direct investment under FEMA.
why_not_A: The 10% limit only matters for securities an FPI is allowed to buy, and unlisted equity isn't one of them.
why_not_C: No SEBI approval brings unlisted equity into the FPI route.
why_not_D: Off-market sales of unlisted shares are allowed for getting out, at FEMA pricing, not for buying in.

citation: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 20(1)(a); Op. Guidelines Part C 4

title: Luxembourg UCITS applies for SWAGAT
fact1_value: Aurelia Global Equity, a Luxembourg SICAV authorised by the CSSF

option_D: No. UCITS have to stay in Category II

Appropriately regulated mutual fund or unit trust open for subscription to retail investors without any specific investor type requirements like accredited investors and complying with the following conditions: i. The applicant operates as a blind pool (i.e. common portfolio) with diversified investors and investments. ii. The contributors to the applicant do not have control over day-to-day operations of the applicant and the investment manager of the applicant is independent from such contributors;
quote_2: II. The applicant being a public retail fund is setup in identified jurisdiction and regulated by the identified statutory authority / regulatory body in such identified jurisdiction. title: GIFT City fund and the residency test
fact1_value: Saffron Bridge Fund, a Category III AIF set up in GIFT IFSC and registered with IFSCA

question: How should the DDP treat the residency and home-regulator tests?
option_A: Reject it, since an Indian-resident entity can't be an FPI
option_B: Skip them, since Reg 4's proviso switches them off for IFSC
option_C: Register it as Category II only, since IFSCA isn't a foreign regulator
option_D: Ask SEBI for a one-off relaxation under Reg 43B
explanation: The proviso to Reg 4 says clauses (a), (d) and (e) don't apply to an applicant incorporated or set up in an IFSC. Those are the resident-Indian bar, the IOSCO or MoU jurisdiction test, and the BIS test for banks. The Explanation to Reg 5 also deems IFSC applicants appropriately regulated. The other tests, such as sanctions and fit and proper, still apply.
why_not_A: The residency bar in Reg 4(a) is one of the clauses the proviso switches off for IFSC applicants.
why_not_C: IFSC applicants are deemed appropriately regulated, so they aren't pushed into Category II for that reason.
why_not_D: No relaxation is needed. The carve-out is already in the regulation.

title: Relying on the global custodian's KYC

option_A: Nothing more; reliance covers everything

option_C: Redo all of the KYC from scratch itself

explanation: For non-PAN KYC documents, a local custodian can rely on KYC by a same-group regulated entity from a FATF country, with an undertaking to produce documents on demand. It must still collect constitution documents and BO declarations, and upload evidence of the reliance to the KRA.

Where this reliance is placed, such entity/ FPI shall provide an undertaking to the effect that the relevant KYC documents, would be submitted to the DDP/ Local Custodian when required by regulator/law enforcement agency/ government departments/ tax authority, etc. However, the Custodian / local intermediary will be required to collect constitution documents and BO related declarations (wherever applicable) of the FPI and also, upload the evidence of KYC reliance on KRA.

KRA will send an email to the requesting intermediary that consent request email has been sent to the authorised representative of the FPI, to enable them to follow up for the consent. e. KRA will permit download of KYC records and information once the consent is received from the authorised representative of the FPI.

title: DDP wants to give up its approval

(1) Any designated depository participant, who has been granted approval under these regulations, desirous of surrendering the approval granted, may make a request for such surrender to the Board. (2) While accepting the surrender under sub-regulation (1), the Board may impose such conditions as it deems fit for the protection of investors or the clients of the designated depository participant or the securities market and such person shall comply with such conditions.

quote_1: 14. An application for grant of approval to act as designated depository participant which is not complete in all respects or is false or misleading in any material particular, shall be deemed to be deficient and shall be liable to be rejected by the Board: Provided that, before rejecting any such application, the applicant shall be given a reasonable opportunity to remove the deficiency, within the time as specified by the Board.

quote_1: (e) the applicant has systems and procedures to comply with the requirements of the Financial Action Task Force Standards, Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Rules prescribed thereunder and the circulars issued from time to time by the Board;

title: Which of these can't an FPI buy?
fact2_value: REIT units, Indian Depository Receipts, exchange-traded index futures, private unlisted company shares
fact4_value: Which one is outside the FPI route?
question: Which is not permitted through the FPI route?
option_A: Units of a listed REIT
option_B: Indian Depository Receipts
option_C: Exchange-traded index futures
option_D: Private unlisted company shares
explanation: Reg 20(1) lets FPIs invest in listed or to-be-listed shares, mutual fund units, CIS units, exchange-traded derivatives, REIT, InvIT and Category III AIF units, IDRs, and permitted debt. Private unlisted shares aren't on the list; buying them is FDI.
why_not_A: REIT units are permitted under Reg 20(1)(e).
why_not_B: Indian Depository Receipts are permitted under Reg 20(1)(f).
why_not_C: Exchange-traded derivatives are permitted under Reg 20(1)(d).
quote_1_source: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 20(1)
quote_1: 20. (1) A foreign portfolio investor shall invest only in the following securities, namely (a) shares, debentures and warrants issued by a body corporate; listed or to be listed on a recognized stock exchange in India; (b) units of schemes launched by mutual funds under Chapter V, VI-A and VI-B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Mutual Fund) Regulations, 1996; (c) units of schemes floated by a Collective Investment Scheme in accordance with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Collective Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999; (d) derivatives traded on a recognized stock exchange; (e) units of real estate investment trusts, infrastructure investment trusts and units of Category III Alternative Investment Funds registered with the Board; (f) Indian Depository Receipts; (g) any debt securities or other instruments as permitted by the Reserve Bank of India for foreign portfolio investors to invest in from time to time; and (h) such other instruments as specified by the Board from time to time.

title: Pre-listing shares after an IPO

quote_1: (2) Where a foreign portfolio investor, prior to commencement of these regulations, holds equity shares in a company whose shares are not listed on any recognised stock exchange, and continues to hold such shares after the initial public offering and listing thereof, such shares shall be subject to lock-in for the same period, if any, as is applicable to shares held by a foreign direct investor placed in similar position, under the policy of the Government of India relating to foreign direct investment for the time being in force.

title: Selling before settlement

question: What does the SOP say to check?
option_A: MAS's list of licensed banks
option_B: OPERA's 'Offers for CIS' listings
option_C: The Singapore company registry
option_D: The fund's own website
explanation: OPERA holds offer documents lodged with MAS. Under 'Offers for CIS', schemes constituted in Singapore are Authorised Schemes and those constituted abroad are Recognised Schemes.
why_not_A: The bank list doesn't show fund status.
why_not_C: The company registry doesn't show retail-fund status.
why_not_D: The SOP points to the regulator's portal.
quote_1_source: CDSSF SOP for SWAGAT-FI, 27 May 2026, Annex B (Singapore)
quote_1: OPERA acts as repository for the offer documents and prospectus lodged or registered with MAS. The schemes constituted in Singapore are called Authorized Schemes (includes Mutual Funds, ETFs and REITs) and the Schemes constituted outside Singapore are called Recognized schemes. The appropriate section in OPERA to be checked for funds is “Offers for CIS”.

title: Canadian mutual fund's retail status
fact2_value: National Instrument 81-102
fact3_value: The rules don't require every mutual fund to be open to retail
fact4_value: How does the DDP confirm retail access?
question: What does the SOP suggest?
option_A: Assume retail access, since it's a mutual fund
option_B: Check SEDAR+ and the simplified prospectus
option_C: Ask the Ontario Securities Commission for a letter
option_D: Retail status can't be confirmed for Canadian funds
explanation: The SOP notes that NI 81-101 doesn't mandate retail access, so the prospectus is used. Funds recognised as a conventional or alternative mutual fund on SEDAR+ that file a simplified prospectus can be treated as public retail funds after checking it.
why_not_A: The SOP marks retail access To Be Verified.
why_not_C: A regulator letter isn't the suggested route.
why_not_D: It can be confirmed from the prospectus.
quote_1_source: CDSSF SOP for SWAGAT-FI, 27 May 2026, Annex B (Canada)
quote_1: While the National Instrument 81-101 does not mandate a Mutual fund to be open to retail public for all mutual funds, the prospectus should be used to verify these details. Generally, funds recognized as Mutual Fund/ETF or RRSP at SEDAR/ SEDAR+, can be considered as Public Retail Fund based on verification from simplified prospectus

title: Malaysian unit trust
fact2_value: Securities Commission Malaysia
fact3_value: Guidelines don't require unit trusts to be open to retail
question: What does the SOP say?
option_A: Nothing; unit trusts are retail funds by law
option_B: Check the prospectus or trust deed
option_C: Malaysian funds can't qualify
option_D: A board resolution from the manager
explanation: The SOP notes that Malaysia's Guidelines on Unit Trust Funds don't mandate retail access, so the prospectus or trust deed is used to check for subscription restrictions.
why_not_A: The SOP marks retail access To Be Verified.
why_not_C: Malaysian unit trusts are listed in Annex B.
why_not_D: A board resolution isn't the suggested evidence.
quote_1_source: CDSSF SOP for SWAGAT-FI, 27 May 2026, Annex B (Malaysia)
quote_1: While the Guidelines on Unit Trust Funds does not mandate a Unit trust to be open to retail public, the prospectus/ trust deed should be used to verify if there are any restrictions on subscriptions

title: GIFT City retail scheme
fact2_value: IFSCA, under the Fund Management Regulations 2025
fact4_value: Can it be a public retail fund for SWAGAT?
question: Does it qualify?
option_A: No. Only foreign jurisdictions are identified in the SOP
option_B: Yes. IFSCA retail schemes are listed
option_C: Only if it also registers in Luxembourg
option_D: Only as Category II
explanation: The SOP's Annex B lists retail schemes under the IFSCA Fund Management Regulations 2025 as meeting all five public retail fund conditions.
why_not_A: GIFT IFSC is specifically listed.
why_not_C: No foreign registration is needed.
why_not_D: Category doesn't decide SWAGAT eligibility.
quote_1_source: CDSSF SOP for SWAGAT-FI, 27 May 2026, Annex B (GIFT IFSC)
quote_1: The scheme is open for subscription to retail investors and is offered pursuant to an offer document filed with IFSCA in accordance with applicable regulations.
citation: SWAGAT SOP 27 May 2026, Annex B (GIFT IFSC)

title: Hong Kong MPF scheme
fact2_value: Hong Kong MPF Schemes Authority
question: Can it use the pension route?
option_A: No. Hong Kong isn't covered
option_B: Yes. MPF and ORSO schemes are listed
option_C: Only as a retail unit trust
option_D: Only if government owned
explanation: Annex C lists Hong Kong's Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority. MPF schemes registered under the MPF Schemes Ordinance and occupational schemes registered under ORSO are retirement schemes for this purpose.
why_not_A: Hong Kong appears in Annex C.
why_not_C: The pension route is available.
why_not_D: Government ownership isn't required for pension funds.
quote_1_source: CDSSF SOP for SWAGAT-FI, 27 May 2026, Annex C (Hong Kong)
quote_1: ORSO schemes and MPF schemes are both retirement protection schemes set up for employees in Hong Kong.
citation: SWAGAT SOP 27 May 2026, Annex C (Hong Kong)

title: Renewing a SWAGAT-FI FPI
fact2_value: First 10-year block ending
question: What's required?
option_A: A full new application with fresh KYC
option_B: Pay US$2,500 and report changes
option_C: Nothing; status is permanent
option_D: Pay US$250 and a no-change declaration
explanation: A SWAGAT-FI continuing for the next 10-year block pays the renewal fee to its DDP (US$2,500 for FPI only) and informs any changes in information submitted earlier.
why_not_A: Renewal isn't a new application.
why_not_C: Renewal is still due every 10 years.
why_not_D: US$250 is the regular Category II fee.
quote_1_source: CDSSF SOP for SWAGAT-FI, 27 May 2026, Section 3 B.4
quote_1: 4. Renewal of SWAGAT-FI: FPIs who wish to continue with their registration for the subsequent block of 10 years, should pay the fees to their DDPs and inform changes in information, if any, as submitted earlier.
citation: SWAGAT SOP 27 May 2026, section 3 B.4–B.5; circular 16 Jan 2026, para 3.3

title: One investor steers the fund
fact1_value: Regulated unit trust, open to retail
fact2_value: One institution holds 60% and directs investment choices
question: Does it meet the retail fund conditions?
option_A: Yes. It's regulated and open to retail investors
option_B: No. The control and independence tests fail
option_C: Yes, if the investor drops below 50%
option_D: Only as a pension fund
explanation: A public retail fund must operate as a blind pool with diversified investors, contributors must not control day-to-day operations, and the manager must be independent of contributors. A dominant investor directing the manager fails these tests.
why_not_A: Being open to retail is only one of five conditions.
why_not_C: The test is control and independence, not a 50% line.
why_not_D: It isn't a pension fund.
quote_1_source: SEBI circular, 16 Jan 2026 (SWAGAT-FI), para 3.2 (vi)(I)(b)
quote_1: b. Appropriately regulated mutual fund or unit trust open for subscription to retail investors without any specific investor type requirements like accredited investors and complying with the following conditions: i. The applicant operates as a blind pool (i.e. common portfolio) with diversified investors and investments. ii. The contributors to the applicant do not have control over day-to-day operations of the applicant and the investment manager of the applicant is independent from such contributors;
